1:
The opening is heard as a deliberate echo, and the echo is pressed for its argument. Lightfoot notes that the phrase stands in the same sense as the first word of the Hebrew Scriptures, and states what he takes the evangelist’s purpose to be: to show that by the Word through whom the creation was perfected the redemption was perfected also, so that the second person of the Trinity became our Redeemer in the fulness of time as he had been our Maker in the beginning of time. Ellicott calls the reference obvious and the more striking because a Jew would habitually name and quote the book of Genesis by that first word; it suits the Hebrew tone of this Gospel, and he thinks it can hardly be that the evangelist wrote his own opening without Moses’s present to his mind. Wesley gives the same cross-reference and draws the contrast it exists for: when all things began to be made by the Word, in the beginning of heaven and earth and this whole frame of created being, the Word already existed without any beginning at all. He adds that the title occurs in the Psalms and in the Greek translators and the Chaldee paraphrase, so the evangelist did not borrow it from Philo. Robertson notes that the Greek is definite although it lacks the article, like our at home or in town and like the Hebrew it renders, and borrows from Westcott the observation that the thought is carried beyond the beginning of creation in time into eternity.

Two of the fathers begin from the difficulty rather than the doctrine. Origen observes that it is not only the Greeks who find many meanings in the word beginning, and sets the reader a method: collect the passages where it occurs and note what it stands for in each, and its range in sacred usage will appear. Hilary states the objection a critic would raise, that a word is the sound of a voice, the enunciation of a thing, the expression of a thought, and that such an utterance might be called eternal because the mind uttering it is eternal; and he turns it by the nature of speech itself, which exists neither before a man speaks nor after but vanishes in the act — so that what has no existence either side of it cannot be what was in the beginning. Chrysostom asks whether the evangelist’s family and country need describing at all, and answers both ways: since it is God by him who speaks, the enquiry looks superfluous, and yet knowing who he was proves necessary.

On the identity of the Word the Reformed voices are the most explicit. Gill insists that what is meant is not the written word but the essential Word of God, and lists the grounds that follow from the text itself — that this Word was in the beginning, was with God and is God, that the creation of all things is ascribed to him, and that he is called the life and the light of men. Calvin reads the whole introduction as an assertion of Christ’s eternal divinity made for a purpose: to show that the restoration of mankind had to be accomplished by the Son of God, since all things were created by his power and he alone breathes life and energy into the creatures so that they keep their condition. Augustine begins instead from his hearers’ capacity, admitting real difficulty in knowing how to speak, since the natural man does not perceive the things of the Spirit and any assembly must hold many who know only according to the flesh. Henry collects two testimonies to the verse’s weight: Augustine’s friend Simplicius had heard a Platonist say these verses deserved writing in letters of gold, and Francis Junius recorded being recovered from loose notions in religion by reading them at hazard.
2:
That the line echoes what precedes it is agreed; why it should is the question. Gill treats the echo as emphasis, marking the weight of three things already delivered — Christ’s eternity, his distinct personality, his proper deity — and argues that the opening phrase governs each of those clauses, so that what is secured is not bare eternal existence but eternal existence alongside the Father. Barnes holds that saying it twice guards the doctrine and makes misunderstanding impossible, since the opening sentence had asserted existence before creation and companionship with God, but had not put in so many words the thing this one nails down. Calvin calls it compression rather than iteration: two earlier clauses are condensed into a short restatement so the point may sink deeper. Wesley reaches the same verdict in a sentence, that three separate assertions are here contracted into one, as though the evangelist had said simply that this Word, who was God, existed from the first and existed beside him.

Ellicott and Robertson both find something gained rather than merely said again. Ellicott grants it is a summary of the three assertions — that the one who was God existed before any creative act, and in that existence stood as a person distinct from him — but insists it goes further, because having reached the thought of a shared nature we now review the earlier steps from that higher vantage. Robertson reads the demonstrative pronoun as a mark of this writer’s manner, repeated for clearness, and borrows the remark that two notions previously kept apart are here welded into a single phrase: originally he was beside God, and afterwards, in time, he came to be beside man. Taken together, Robertson says, the words assert pre-existence before the incarnation, personality, and deity at once.

Hilary alone describes reading it as a relief. Having met the claim that the Word was God, he confesses that the strangeness and fearfulness of such speech disturbed him, the prophets having declared the Deity to be one; and he says the fisherman then discloses the scheme of so great a mystery, referring everything to a single source without dishonour, without cancelling the person, and without any note of time — the Only-begotten standing with the one unbegotten from whom he derives.
3:
How wide the claim runs is settled first. Barnes takes the expression for the universe and refuses to limit it to any part of it, since it properly covers everything that exists, the vast masses of material worlds and all the creatures and things, great or small, that compose them. Ellicott reads the movement of the passage, that from the person of the Word we are guided to his creative work, with the first chapter of Genesis still in mind but now carrying a fuller meaning: all things came into existence through the pre-existent Word, and of everything that now exists nothing came into being apart from him. Gill treats the clause as proof of all that has gone before at once — that he was in the beginning, was with the Father, and was God — since none of it could stand if the making of all things were not his; and he rules out the narrower reading that would confine it to the new creation. Clarke draws the inference that the chapter forces: in Genesis God is said to have created all things and in this verse Christ is, and the same unerring Spirit spoke in Moses and in the evangelists, so that Christ and the Father are one. He then closes the escape, that to say Christ made all things by a power delegated from God is not merely wrong but impossible, given what creation means.

The negative clause is read as a deliberate guard. Chrysostom explains it twice over. It is added lest, hearing that all things were made by him, we should suppose only the things Moses had spoken of were meant, where in fact nothing is excepted that can be known either by the senses or by the understanding; and on a second reading it is added lest the first clause be suspected of referring only to the miracles the other evangelists had related. Chrysostom elsewhere sets the two writers side by side: Moses at the opening of the older Scriptures speaks of the objects of sense and enumerates them at length, the heaven and the earth, then light, a second heaven, the stars and the kinds of living creatures, where this evangelist does not delay over particulars at all.

Origen returns to the word he had been examining and now narrows it. Many meanings of the term had offered themselves; the question is which to adopt here, and he dismisses in turn the sense connected with transition, and with a road and its length, and the sense connected with an origin, as none of them serving the text — though he allows that one might think of another. The method is the same he used before, settling a word by eliminating its possible senses rather than by asserting one.
4:
Whose life is meant, and on what terms he holds it, is settled first. Gill distinguishes the senses and insists on the strongest: there was in the Word a divine life, the same as the Father’s and the Spirit’s, held not by gift nor by derivation nor by communication but originally, independently and from eternity. Barnes connects the clause to what precedes, since one part of the creation just ascribed to the Word consisted in breathing into man the breath of life, and God is called the living God because he is the fountain of life — an attribute here assigned to Christ. Ellicott reads the movement the same way, that the calling of life into its varied forms leads the reader up to the source of it, which is in the Word by original being, whereas even the highest creature received his by being breathed into. He adds that the term here carries no limitation at all. Robertson states it as the governing claim, that the power which creates and sustains life throughout the universe is the Word himself, and notes the same claim made to Martha later in this Gospel.

Calvin extends the thought from creation to maintenance. Hitherto, he says, the evangelist has taught what was done by the Word; he now attributes to him in the same manner the preservation of what was created, as if to say that the making of the world displayed not a sudden exercise of power which soon passed away, but a power manifested in the steady and regular order of nature. Theophylact guards against a misreading in the other direction: having said that life was in him, lest anyone suppose the Word was without life, the evangelist now shows that the life meant is spiritual, and the light of all reasonable creatures — not a light of the senses but an intellectual one, illuminating the soul itself. Augustine is quoted beside him for the limit of it, that life of itself gives illumination to men and not to cattle, since they have no rational souls.

Two of them read the clause as a transition to redemption. Lightfoot says the evangelist moves from the creation by the Word to the redemption of the world by the same Word: having declared that all things were made by him, he now shows how he restored life to man when he lay dead in trespasses and sins. Clarke reports that many manuscripts, versions and fathers attach the words to the preceding verse, so that the sense runs that what was made had life in it, and this life was the light of men; and he draws the distinction that reading forces, between the principle of life in everything made, whether vegetable or animal or intellectual, and this life which is something further. Wesley compresses both halves into a line, that he was the foundation of life to every living thing as well as of being to all that is, and that the essential life and giver of life was also the fountain of wisdom and holiness and happiness to man in his original state.
5:
What the darkness is gets three different answers. Clarke lists them as alternatives — the heathen world, the Jewish people, and the fallen spirit of man. Barnes takes the word in its usual biblical sense of ignorance or guilt or misery and applies it here to a wicked and ignorant people, so that the shining means Christ came to teach a benighted world. Gill describes the darkness from the inside, as the condition into which sin brought men’s minds, naturally in the dark about the nature and perfections of God, about sin and its consequences, about Christ and salvation, about the Spirit’s work on the soul and about the Scriptures themselves — man having been created a knowing creature and having lost it. Lightfoot gives the darkness a different reference altogether, making it the cloudy types and shadows of the law and the obscurity of the prophets, among which this light of promise shone.

What the second verb means divides them further. Clarke prefers to render it prevented or hindered, citing Wakefield and the judicious note that even in the midst of the world’s ignorance and idolatry this light was not extinguished. Lightfoot takes the same line for his own reading, that the dark things did not so cloud and suppress the light as to keep it from breaking out, and yet did not so comprehend it that there was no absolute necessity for something further. Augustine prefers to keep the ordinary sense and explains the failure by the hearer rather than the light: the life is the light of men, but foolish hearts cannot receive it, being so encumbered with sins that they cannot see it — and lest anyone think no light is near him because he cannot see it, the evangelist adds this clause. The illustration Augustine offers is a blind man standing in the sun, with the sun present to him and he absent from the sun.

Origen uses the verse for a question about the Son’s substance. The Saviour is here called simply light, while in this same writer’s epistle God is called light; and it has been maintained that this proves the Son no different in substance from the Father. Origen reports a closer and, he thinks, sounder judgment on the other side, which distinguishes the light that shines in darkness and is not overtaken by it from light considered absolutely — so that the inference from the shared word does not go through as quickly as it appears to.
6:
The change of verb is where the exegetes begin. Ellicott points out that the word is the same one used of the things that were made, set deliberately against the timeless was of the opening lines, so that it signifies coming into being as against original existence; and he notes that man is likewise set emphatically against the Word. Robertson reads it as a definite event breaking a long darkness, with the same verb as before, and parses the participle for sent as a perfect passive, the preposition carrying the sense of from the side of God. Barnes states the purpose of the paragraph, that the evangelist is showing John the Baptist was not the Messiah and stating the true nature of his office, since many had supposed he was the Christ; what is admitted is that he was divinely commissioned.

That the forerunner was a man, and not more, is insisted on. Gill says he was neither the Word nor an angel but a man, though an extraordinary one — conceived of a barren woman, born when both parents were advanced in years, and leaping for joy in the womb at Mary’s salutation. Augustine makes the same point serve the argument about Christ: what has gone before concerns his divinity, and he came to us in the form of man, but of such a man that the Godhead was concealed within him, and therefore a great man was sent ahead to testify by his witness that this one was more than man. Theophylact is quoted beside him for the negative, that the herald was not an angel. Chrysostom draws the practical conclusion from the phrase about his being sent: having spoken in the introduction of urgent things concerning God the Word, the evangelist comes in order to the herald, and now that we hear he was sent from God we are not to imagine any of his words are mere man’s words.

Two further voices treat the sending as a question in its own right. Origen observes that whoever is sent is sent from somewhere to somewhere, and sets the careful student to ask both; the destination, he says, is plain on the face of the story, since he was sent to Israel and to those willing to hear him. Calvin reads the paragraph as the beginning of the narrative proper, where the evangelist starts to discourse on the manner in which the Son of God was manifested in flesh; and he explains why a herald is brought in at all, that none may doubt the eternal Sonship — for Christ did not merely exhibit himself to be seen by men but chose also to be made known by another’s testimony. Augustine, preaching through the Gospel in course, adds a word about his own method, that it is fitting to treat the text without omitting any portion, so that both preacher and hearers may be nourished from the same source.
7:
What the office amounted to is stated plainly and then filled in. Ellicott lays the stress on the noun, which he takes for the general object of the man’s coming and specially for his attestation of the Light; and since the purpose of evidence is conviction, the clause about all men believing means believing by his means. Robertson agrees this was the aim of the Baptist’s whole ministry, parses the final clause as sharpening the phrase before it, and remarks that both the noun and its verb are commoner in this writer than in all the rest of the New Testament together. Gill reduces the matter to a sentence, that the end of his being despatched and the design of his arrival were precisely this. Barnes supplies the work that lay beneath the title: he was to prepare the people’s minds for receiving Christ, to lead them by repentance back to God, and to identify the Messiah to Israel when he appeared.

Clarke sets out what was actually attested, in its parts. The man declared Jesus to be the true light, which is to say the genuine teacher of the road to the kingdom of glory, and the lamb or sacrifice of God appointed to carry away the world’s sin; and on that footing he summoned men to trust him for the pardon of their sins. The summons, on Clarke’s reading, is no separate transaction but the very shape the attestation took, so that preaching and pointing are one act.

Origen turns the clause against a party rather than toward a doctrine. Certain dissenters from the Church’s teaching, while professing faith in Christ, have wanted a second being alongside the Creator, as their scheme requires; and they are therefore unable to grant that his advent was predicted by the prophets. Origen notes the lengths to which they go in consequence. What embarrasses such a system is precisely a herald commissioned by the same God who commissioned the prophets, since his errand ties the new announcement to the old one — which is why the sentence is worth their trouble to explain away.
8:
Why the denial has to be repeated is the question, and the answers concern the Baptist’s reputation rather than his doctrine. Ellicott explains that it was necessary to restate his position in an emphatic form, because for the first time in four centuries a great teacher had appeared in Israel: the circumstances of his birth and life had caught the attention of the masses, and his bold message rang like the cry of another Elias. Calvin puts it more sharply still — so far was the man from needing commendation that the evangelist has to enter a caution, lest his excessive brightness should obscure the glory of Christ; some gazed so eagerly on him that they neglected Christ, as a man enraptured with the dawn might not deign to turn his eyes toward the sun itself.

The distinction being drawn is one of article rather than of kind. Robertson notes that the pronoun singles the man out, and that he genuinely was a light, as this Gospel says elsewhere and as all believers are, but not the light; he observes too that the Greek supplies no verb in the second clause, which must be filled from the sentence before. Gill works the same distinction into a series of concessions: the man was a light, the forerunner of the sun of righteousness and the morning star of the Gospel day, with great light in him — he knew the Messiah was at hand and declared it, knew him personally at the baptism and pointed him out to others. The denial therefore withdraws nothing that belonged to him; it withholds only what belonged to another, and the whole force of the sentence lies in the definite article it refuses him.

Ellicott measures the revival that made the caution necessary. Men of the least likely classes — Pharisee and Sadducee, publican and soldier — were brought to ask what they should do; and he quotes a publican writing at the time for the scale of it, that Jerusalem and all Judaea and the whole region round Jordan went out to him and were baptized, confessing their sins. The extent of it fails to impress us, Ellicott remarks, only because it passed into the greater movement that followed. Calvin draws the same distinction over the word itself: all the godly are called lights, being enlightened by the Spirit so that they both see for themselves and guide others by their example, and the apostles are called so particularly, going before with the torch of the Gospel to scatter the world’s darkness — whereas here the evangelist is speaking of the only and eternal source of illumination.
9:
What the epithet excludes is where they divide. Barnes reads it as excluding falsehood: not an uncertain or dangerous guide but one real and steady and worthy of confidence, a counterfeit beacon on the shore being precisely what runs ships onto rocks. Robertson renders the Greek as the genuine article, set against the lamps wreckers hung out, and calls it the dependable radiance that guides. Calvin denies any contrast with the Baptist here and makes the term separate Christ from every other luminary, lest the title seem to belong to him in common with angels or men: whatever is bright in heaven or earth borrows its splendour elsewhere, where he shines from himself. Gill instead piles up the reach of that shining, calling him the fountain from which every creature draws illumination, who lit the dark earth at the first and spoke brightness out of nothing, and who enlightens men below, angels above, and the saints together.

The clause about every man is the hard one, and it is handled four ways. Clarke takes it of the intellect: as Christ is the spring of all wisdom, whatever wisdom is in man comes from him, the human understanding being a ray of his brightness and reason itself springing from this eternal Reason. Wesley takes it of conscience, what is commonly called natural conscience, pointing out at least the general lines of good and evil, and adds that the light would shine on to the perfect day if man did not hinder it. Lightfoot takes the phrase about coming into the world as a Jewish idiom for all men living, and supports it from sayings in which all that come into the world are spoken of collectively. Ellicott doubts the received rendering altogether and thinks a better sense is got by reading that the true Light which lightens every man was coming into the world — that is, was manifesting itself at the very time when the Baptist was bearing witness and men were mistaking the lamp for the light. Robertson notes the same construction and the emphatic position of the verb at the head of the sentence, while allowing the other reading possible.

Augustine and Chrysostom both explain why the verse comes where it does. Augustine says the evangelist here shows for himself what light it was that the Baptist attested. Chrysostom gives the reason more exactly: having said that the witness came and was sent, the writer guards against anyone inferring from the recent arrival of the witness that the one witnessed to was equally recent. Chrysostom also pauses over his own practice of expounding piece by piece rather than pouring out everything at once, on the ground that what is set before hearers in succession is the easier to retain — as in building, where one who lays fresh stones before the first are settled constructs badly.
10:
The three clauses are read as a descending series of reproaches. Augustine explains why the one who lightens every man had to come in the flesh: while he was here in his divinity alone the foolish and blind and unrighteous could not discern him, being the very people of whom it was said that the darkness did not comprehend it. The incarnation, on that reading, answers the failure recorded earlier in the chapter rather than introducing a new theme. Origen is quoted beside him for a comparison that makes the same point from the side of the perceiver.

Theophylact uses the second clause against two parties at once. That the world was made by him overthrows the insane notion of the Manichee, who holds the world to be the work of a malignant creator, and equally the opinion of the Arian, who holds the Son of God to be a creature; neither position survives a sentence which makes the world’s maker the one who came into it. Augustine is quoted in the same place for the plain sense of the words, that the earth and sky and sea and all that is in them are what the world means here, so that nothing is exempted from the making.

Gill keeps to the paradox the verse states rather than to the controversies it settles. The maker was present in what he had made, and the thing made did not recognise its maker; which is the sharpest form the chapter has yet given to the failure first mentioned in the clause about darkness, since ignorance of a stranger is one thing and ignorance of the author of one’s own being quite another. He denies the clause refers to the incarnation at all, since the verb denotes past existence through all the time since the world was made, and the world here is the world at large as opposed to Judaea in the verse following; the presence meant is that of essence, filling the whole world, of power, upholding it, and of providence, ordering its affairs.

The moderns divide over that very point. Barnes takes the clause of the incarnation and the dwelling among men, and reads the mention of the making as placed here to sharpen what follows, that men did not receive him; he lists the two proofs they had, the miracles and teaching given while he was among them, and the bare fact that the world was his own workmanship. Robertson agrees with Gill on the tense, an imperfect of continuous existence before the incarnation, and parses the last verb as what one grammarian called a negative aorist, a refusal or failure to recognise. Clarke extends the presence backward through the whole history, governing the universe, regulating his Church, speaking by the prophets and appearing as the messenger of Jehovah to the patriarchs; and he distinguishes failing to know from declining to acknowledge, since the Jewish rulers knew well enough that he was a teacher come from God and chose not to own him. Calvin turns the whole into a charge of ingratitude, asking what is more unreasonable than to draw water from a running stream and never think of the fountain it flows from. Ellicott states what ought to have happened instead: the world in its highest creature, man, had the spiritual power to see the true Light and ought to have recognised him, and in that recognition would have exercised its true power and found its highest good — but it was sense-bound and lost the perception.
11:
Whose own is meant is the whole question, and four answers are given. Barnes takes it of the land, called his because it was his birthplace and the chosen country where God had delighted to dwell and show favour, a land over which his laws had been extended. Clarke reads the Greek more domestically, as those of his own family and city and country, his own citizens and brethren and subjects, and supports both senses from the Greek translators and from Josephus. Robertson insists the first phrase is neuter plural, his own things, and points to the identical idiom later in the Gospel where the beloved disciple takes the mother of Jesus to his own home — the world having been the Word’s own home, since he made it. Gill narrows it against two readings at once: not all the world, who are his own by right of creation, since these are set in contrast with the world; and not the elect either, though they are his own, because the coming described is a particular favour not granted to all. Wesley compresses the distinction into a line, the first own being country and city and temple, the second a people.

How the verse stands to the one before it is the second point. Ellicott marks the change from was to came as a passage to the historic advent, and then declines to let that exclude what went before, since the advent was the more distinct act of which every earlier appearance and revelation of God had been a foreshadowing. Chrysostom draws the same line between the dispensations: when the evangelist said the world did not know him he was speaking of the times of the old dispensation, where what follows belongs to the time of the preaching. Theophylact offers the alternatives without choosing, that his own may mean either the world or Judaea, which he had chosen; and Augustine supplies the ground of the first reading in a phrase, that all things were made by him.

The refusal is where the indignation gathers. Calvin calls it a display of the absolutely desperate wickedness and malice of men, and of their execrable impiety, that when the Son of God was manifested in flesh to the very nation God had separated from the others to be his own heritage, he was not received; and Calvin notes that this clause too has had various explanations. Clarke puts the failure as a refusal to acknowledge rather than an inability to perceive. Cyril sets the rejection against the longing that preceded it, that the Father did not disregard the perishing of our race but sent his Son as a healer, and that one of the prophets had said the Lord whom they sought would come suddenly to his own temple — which is the place where he was not received.
12:
What receiving means is defined by the clause that follows it. Gill says the latter half of the verse explains the first, since faith is a receiving of him as the Word and Son of God, as Messiah and Saviour and Redeemer, and a receiving of grace out of his fulness. Barnes says the same more briefly, that to receive him here means to believe on him, and notes who did: not the great mass nor the scribes and Pharisees, but a few in his lifetime and many more after his death. Wesley makes the timing immediate — the moment they believe they are sons, and because they are sons God sends the Spirit of his Son into their hearts. Robertson parses the aorist as effective, as many as did receive him, and sets it in deliberate contrast with the phrase about his own just before, calling it exceptional action on the part of the disciples and other believers.

The word rendered power is corrected by three of them. Clarke prefers privilege, or honour, or dignity, or right, and calls the sonship the greatest privilege the Divine Being can confer on this side of eternity, held through the blood of Christ by those who accept him as the Gospel offers him. Lightfoot renders it that he empowered them, giving them the privilege and liberty and dignity of being called and becoming the sons of God, and marks the change it brought: Israel had once been the son and the firstborn, where now the adoption stands open and free to all. Barnes likewise thinks another word renders the Greek more appropriately than power does.

Ellicott and Calvin both read the verse as a correction of the national reckoning. Ellicott observes that the phrase is at once narrower and wider than his own: narrower, because the nation as such rejected him while individuals in it accepted him; wider, because not individuals of that nation only, since all who accept him according to their light and means receive the same gift. Calvin says the evangelist exalts the believing above heaven itself, lest anyone be held back by the stumbling-block of the Jews’ contempt, and finds an implied contrast in the universal term, since the Jews were carried away by a blind vaunting of their descent.
13:
What the birth is, and what the three denials exclude, is the substance of the verse. Gill identifies it as regeneration — a being born again or from above, quickened by the Spirit and grace of God, Christ formed in a man, a partaking of the divine nature. Barnes says the same and draws out the negative: they did not become God’s children by virtue of their natural birth, nor because they were Jews, nor because they were descended from pious parents. Robertson parses the verb as a first aorist passive, who were begotten, and sets spiritual generation against physical; he notes the plural of the first noun as common in the classics and the older Scriptures, and confesses it is not clear why it should be plural unless the blood of both parents is meant. Clarke offers a different account of the plural, that Hebrew uses it to mark the dignity or excellence of a thing, so that what is excluded is descent from a distinguished or illustrious ancestry. Wesley takes the three clauses one by one, not by descent from Abraham, not by natural generation, not by any man adopting them, but of God by his Spirit.

Lightfoot raises a prior question nobody else asks. It may be doubted, he says, whether the evangelist is here opposing regeneration to natural generation at all, or only to the particular ways in which the Jews imagined men were made sons of God; expositors treat the former largely, and he proposes to consider the latter — so that the denials would be aimed at specific rabbinic claims rather than at physical descent as such.

Ellicott explains why the verse is needed at all. The result of receiving him remains to be accounted for: how could such people become sons of God? The word used just before excludes the notion of adoption and asserts the natural relation of child to father, which is exactly what the nation claimed through its descent from Abraham — and the answer is that Abraham’s children are those who are of his faith. Cyril guards the term from the other direction, that the Father, being very God, begat the Son like himself, very God, not in the way teachers beget disciples nor in the way Paul could say he had begotten men through the Gospel; in that case one who was no son by nature became a son by discipleship, where in the former the sonship is of another order altogether.
14:
The change of verb is the first thing marked, and it is marked as decisive. Gill identifies the subject as the same Word of the preceding verses, no other than the Son of God, and makes the Trinitarian point exactly: neither the Father nor the Holy Ghost was made flesh, as is here said, but the Son only. Clarke says that the very person who was in the beginning, who was with God and who was God, in the fulness of time became incarnate by the power of the Holy Ghost in the womb of the virgin. Barnes settles the meaning of the second noun from usage across the Scriptures, that it denotes human nature or man, so that the Word was made man — what is commonly expressed by saying he became incarnate. Ellicott draws the line against a party: they were not, as certain men of that age held, dealing with an appearance of a body, and he puts the reciprocity in a sentence, that man came to be a son of God because the Son of God became man.

Chrysostom connects the two halves of the verse as gift and consequence. Having said that we are made sons of God in no other way than because the Word was made flesh, the evangelist mentions a second gift, that we saw his glory — a glory we could never have seen had he not, by his alliance with humanity, become visible to us; for if men could not endure to look on lesser things, the unveiled sight would have been beyond them. Ellicott reads the whole clause as evidence working backwards: the reality of the moral change wrought in those who believed recalls, and is itself proof of, the reality of the thing they believed in.

The glory itself is defined by what it was not. Lightfoot says the word here carries the sense of what was worthy, so that they saw a glory such as became the only-begotten Son of God; and he denies it glittered in any worldly pomp or grandeur of the kind the nation fondly dreamed their Messiah would display. That reading leaves the clause consistent with everything the chapter has said about a presence unrecognised: a glory proper to the only-begotten could be beheld by those who received him while the world that was made by him saw nothing to remark.
15:
The verse returns to the forerunner, and the return is explained. Barnes notes that the evangelist, having stated that the Word became incarnate, now appeals to the Baptist’s testimony to show that the one so incarnate was the Messiah. Alcuin says the same of the structure: it had been said earlier that a man was sent to bear witness, and here the forerunner’s own words are given definitely, declaring both the excellence of his human nature and the eternity of his Godhead. Gill reduces it to a clause, that this was the man’s office and the business he was sent for. Chrysostom reads the insertion as forestalling an objection, as though the evangelist were saying that nobody should suppose the claim rests on his own word alone.

The tense of the verbs is pressed by three of them. Ellicott prefers the present throughout, that he beareth witness and crieth, noting that the second verb is past in form but present in meaning, because the writer thinks of the testimony as ever present and ever forceful. Robertson calls the first a historical or dramatic present and a characteristic word of this writer, and treats the sentence as a parenthesis. Calvin makes the same observation about the present tense and draws from it a continued act rather than a finished one, so that the preaching is represented as still sounding.

How the cry was uttered, and when, is filled in from the circumstances. Clarke has him deeply convinced of the importance and truth of his subject and delivering his testimony with the utmost zeal and earnestness. Wesley has him crying with joy and confidence, and settles the chronology carefully: he had said this before the baptism, although he did not then know him in person, came to know him at the baptism, and afterwards cried that this was the one he had spoken of. Henry marks the manner as part of the evidence, that he cried rather than merely said it. Cyril explains why such a man was fit for the office, having been filled with the Holy Ghost from his mother’s womb and sanctified for this very cause, that he might baptize the Lord — not giving the Spirit himself but announcing good tidings of the one who gives him.
16:
Whose words these are is the first dispute. Gill holds they are not the Baptist’s but the evangelist’s, carrying on his own account of Christ after inserting the testimony, and connected with the earlier statement that he was full of grace and truth. Ellicott argues the same from the language, that the fulness and the grace are key-words of the preceding verse and that the phrase about all of us marks the speaker; he adds that fulness is a technical theological term which recurs in this sense elsewhere. Origen takes the opposite view and says the point has escaped many: he treats the words as a continuation of the Baptist’s testimony, against those who think the apostle resumes speaking here, on the ground that the discourse would otherwise break off suddenly and unseasonably. Clarke goes further than either and reorders the text, putting this verse in the place of the one before it and moving that one down, so that the Baptist’s testimony may be properly connected.

What was received, and what the odd phrase about grace means, is handled next. Barnes recalls that Christ was said to be full of grace and truth, and takes the disciples to have derived from that abundance the grace to understand the plan of salvation, to preach the gospel and to live as they did. Clarke glosses the fulness as the plenitude of grace and mercy by which the atonement was made. Lightfoot gives the second phrase a particular turn: all who conversed with him and saw his glory received grace and truth of his fulness, and more than that, they received grace toward the propagation of grace, which is to say the grace of apostleship, that they might dispense it to others.

Chrysostom returns to the question the earlier clause had raised, how one who came after in the order of preaching could be before and more glorious; he recalls the answer already given, that he was before him, and says the Baptist was not content with that single reason but added more. The effect is to make the testimony cumulative rather than a single assertion repeated, which is why the evangelist can build his own statement about the fulness directly onto it.
17:
The contrast is read as two pairs set deliberately against each other. Robertson notes the prepositions, that the law was given through Moses as the intermediate agent of God, and that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ as the intermediate agent of the Father; he marks the second verb as the historical event, the beginning of Christianity. Wesley makes the choice of words the whole point and says no philosopher or poet or orator ever chose his so accurately: the law was given by Moses, where grace was by Jesus Christ — the reason for each being that the law of Moses was not his own. Barnes identifies the first term as the Old Testament economy, the institutions under which the Jews lived, framed by Moses as God’s servant; and he recalls that the law works wrath and was attended with many things that were not grace. Gill divides it into the moral and the ceremonial, and gives the moral a longer history: given to Adam in innocence, broken and almost lost out of men’s minds and memories, and then given through Moses in a new edition in writing.

Why the comparison is made at all is Calvin’s subject. He calls the verse an anticipation, meeting an objection likely to arise, since Moses stood so high in Jewish esteem that they could hardly receive anything differing from him; the evangelist therefore shows how far that ministry fell below this power. Ellicott reads the connecting word as explanatory and traces the thought back: the idea of grace and truth was already present in the preceding verse, where the fulness of those attributes was beheld in the glory of the Word, and what this verse adds is the revealing of them, the removing of the veil. Clarke makes the same transition the subject of the book, that grace and truth, already mentioned, were to be its matter, and came to all mankind through the one here named. Clarke is careful about the first half as well, that Moses received the law from God and it was through him that it reached the Jews, so that even the giver was himself a receiver — which is the asymmetry Wesley had fixed on, and the reason the two verbs of the verse cannot be exchanged.
18:
What the denial excludes is narrowed carefully. Gill takes it of the Father, whose voice was never heard nor shape seen by angels or men, and then faces the apparent exceptions, that Jacob and Moses and the elders of Israel and Manoah are said to have seen God, and Job expected to see him with his bodily eyes. Robertson settles it by the mode of seeing: no one has ever seen God with the human physical eye, which is what the evangelist means, God being invisible as the older Scriptures say and as Paul calls him. Wesley puts the same distinction in a line, that no man has seen him with bodily eyes, yet believers see him with the eye of faith. Clarke allows the earlier manifestations their place — Moses and others heard the voice and saw the cloud and the fire that symbolised the presence — and insists that such a manifestation as had now taken place in the person of Jesus Christ had never been exhibited before. Cyril states the ground of the impossibility, that the incorporeal cannot be subject to bodily sight, and takes the Only-begotten’s own words as the testimony to it.

Why the denial stands here is explained by its use. Barnes thinks it is made to show the superiority of this revelation over any previous dispensation, so that Jesus had an intimate knowledge of God which neither Moses nor any ancient prophet possessed. Ellicott keeps the primary reference to Moses and then widens it, that the words hold good of every attempt to bridge the gap from the human standpoint, since the full knowledge of truth is one with the revelation of God and no man has ever had that knowledge. Calvin calls the clause most appropriately added to confirm what precedes, since the knowledge of God is the door by which we enter the enjoyment of all blessings, and since it is by Christ alone that God makes himself known, from which it follows that we must seek everything from Christ.

The closing phrase is weighed for how much it claims. Chrysostom says that to dwell in the bosom is much more than simply to see, because one who merely sees has no thorough knowledge of what he sees, where one who dwells there knows everything — which is how the earlier denial is to be heard. Wesley says the expression denotes the highest unity and the most intimate knowledge. Origen, meanwhile, disputes the attribution of the preceding verse, reporting that Heracleon made it a declaration of the disciple rather than the Baptist, and calling that an unreasonable supposition, since the connection runs naturally enough if the words about receiving of his fulness are the Baptist’s own.
19:
The word rendered record is corrected first. Barnes warns that it means testimony, in whatever way given, and not written evidence as the English word now commonly suggests, since the Baptist’s was given without writing. Robertson calls it the witness and notes the evangelist has twice alluded to it already before setting it down here as the most important thing to add after the prologue. Gill reads the verse as the opening of a large and full account of that testimony, which had been hinted at before and named as the man’s work and office and the very end of his being sent. Clarke puts the force of it in a clause, that he persisted in the assertion, testifying to the Jews that this Jesus was the Christ.

Who sent, and who were sent, is supplied from the circumstances. Henry identifies the senders as the Jews at Jerusalem, that is the great council, and the delegation as the messengers they despatched to examine him. Wesley agrees that it was probably the great council. Barnes explains why such a deputation came at all, since the man’s fame was great and had spread widely. Ellicott pauses over the term Jews itself, which belonged originally to the members of one tribe and was extended after the Captivity to the whole nation; and he notes that the narrative is tied to the prologue by this very record, which both share, so that the sentence opens with a conjunction. Calvin marks the step up in the evidence: hitherto the evangelist has related the preaching, and he now comes down to a more illustrious testimony, delivered to ambassadors so that they might carry it back to Jerusalem, and in which the man openly confessed for what purpose God had sent him.

Origen and Theophylact both place the passage in the sequence of testimonies. Origen calls this the second testimony of the Baptist to Christ, the first having begun with the words about the one of whom he spoke and ended with the declaring of him. Theophylact reads the arrangement differently, that having introduced the testimony about being preferred before him, the evangelist now adds when that testimony was given. Chrysostom turns to the motive of the senders rather than the sent, and opens on envy as a dreadful and pernicious thing which harms the envier first, like a mortal venom seated deep in the soul, and does its objects comparatively little damage. Augustine praises the man questioned instead, that in proportion as he was greater than those born of women and more humble in acknowledging the Lord, he obtained the grace of being the Bridegroom’s friend, zealous for the Bridegroom and not for himself.
20:
The doubled verb is noticed by everyone and explained in two ways. Robertson parses the construction and the old verb behind it, which means to say the same thing, and notes the continued stringing of clauses by the conjunction. Ellicott compares the style with an earlier verse and prefers the reading that throws the pronoun into the most emphatic place, so that the answer runs that it is not he who is the Messiah; he takes their question, then, as expressing the general expectation rather than mere curiosity. Clarke calls the phrasing a common mode of Jewish speech and reads the sense as a renunciation, the man putting himself aside so that Jesus may be all in all — for though God had highly honoured him and given him peculiar influence in his work, he reckoned he had nothing but what he had received. Gill describes the manner of it, that he declared freely and without reserve, in the plainest and strongest terms, before all the people, and neither retracted the confession nor drew his words in again.

Barnes draws an argument from the denial itself. The confession proves the man was no impostor: his reputation was wide, the nation was expecting the Messiah, and multitudes were ready to believe that he was the one — so that an impostor in his position had every opportunity and every motive to accept the title offered him. What he did instead is the strongest evidence of his honesty, since the one thing a pretender does not do is refuse the credit pressed upon him.

Origen, commenting in this place, turns aside to the apostolic writings, observing that Paul, made fit to be a minister of the new covenant not of the letter but of the spirit, and having carried the Gospel from Jerusalem round about to Illyricum, nevertheless did not write to all the churches he taught, and wrote only briefly to some of those he did address. The remark bears on the Baptist by analogy: the measure of a commission is not the volume of what its holder claims for himself.
21:
Why Elijah should be the next guess is explained from expectation. Barnes says the Jews looked for Elijah to appear before the Messiah came, and supposed it would be the real Elijah returned from heaven — which is the sense in which the Baptist denied being him, though in another sense he did not. Gill reports the same notion, that the prophet would come in person a little before the Messiah, and notes he had been translated soul and body to heaven. Clarke traces the belief to the scribes, who had taught it themselves and supported it by a literal construction of the closing prophecy of Malachi. Wesley makes the distinction exactly, that he was not that Elijah of whom they spoke. Calvin asks why they name Elijah rather than Moses, and answers from the same prophecy, that they had learned the forerunner would be the morning star announcing the Messiah’s approach; but he adds that the question rests on a false opinion they had long held.

The second question has its own background. Clarke identifies the prophet as the one Moses spoke of in Deuteronomy, and Wesley says the same in a line. Lightfoot takes it differently, as asking whether he were one of the old prophets risen again, and supplies the rabbinic doctrine behind the question, that the spirit of prophecy departed from Israel after the deaths of Zechariah and Malachi — so that any prophet now appearing would have to be a returning one. Ellicott reads the opening words not as asking what he is but as expressing surprise at the previous answer and passing on impatiently to the alternative. Robertson calls the Elijah question the next inevitable one and marks the argumentative force of the connecting particle.

Origen faces the difficulty the denial creates. Nobody can fail to remember, he says, what Jesus himself says of this man, that if they will receive it, this is Elijah who is to come; and the question is how the Baptist comes to say the opposite to those who ask him. The tension is not resolved by softening either saying, but by observing what each is answering — which is the same move the moderns make when they distinguish the person of Elijah from his office.
22:
The question is read as a last resort. Gill explains the sequence: so far he had answered only in negatives, telling them who he was not — not the Christ, not Elijah, not that prophet — and they now press him for a positive account. Ellicott puts it as an exhausted list, that he has given the No to every idea they had formed of him, so that nothing remains but to draw a definite statement out of him or go back to their senders empty handed. Origen paraphrases the delegation’s speech to the same effect, that they had a surmise what he was and came to learn whether it was so. Robertson notes that the question is the same one they began with, and marks the inferential force of the particle, which in this writer is often merely transitional but here draws a conclusion.

Clarke supplies the official position they were in. These Pharisees were probably a deputation from the great council, whose members, hearing of the success of the Baptist’s preaching, were puzzled what to make of him and genuinely wanted to hear from the man himself. On that reading the clause about giving an answer is not a threat but an embarrassment: a body that had sent inquirers could not report back a series of denials, and the questioners are asking to be given something they can carry home.

Robertson’s grammatical notes press on the wording. The question is put more briefly than at the first asking, the purpose clause with its subjunctive makes the reply something they must carry away, and the dative plural participle keeps the senders in view as the party to be satisfied. On the closing clause he observes that this time they opened the door wide without giving any hint at all — the earlier questions had each named a figure and invited a yes, where this one names nothing and leaves the whole field to him. Origen’s paraphrase ends in the same place: it remains for them to hear his own account of himself, so that they may report that answer to those who sent them.
23:
What the answer concedes about himself is the point every one of them fastens on. Ellicott observes that he is still giving the No: they think of his person and his work, and he thinks of neither, his eye being fixed on the coming One, in whose presence his own personality has no existence — he is a voice, not something to be inquired about but something to be heard. Gill notes that the other evangelists cite the same words and apply them to the Baptist, where here the application is his own, made in his own mouth. Robertson marks the defective verb and identifies the quotation as from Isaiah, noting that the Synoptics apply it to him while here he claims it.

Calvin reads the self-description as a definition of all true ministry, since a voice exists only to convey what is spoken through it and vanishes when the word has been delivered. On that footing the answer the delegation found so unsatisfying is the most exact thing the man could have said: they wanted a title and he gave them a function, and the function is wholly relative to another. Barnes and Clarke both pass the clause on to their notes at the parallel places rather than repeat the exposition, which leaves the force of it where the Baptist put it — on the one crying rather than on the crier.

Calvin presses the wilderness itself. Isaiah gives that name to the desolation of the Church, which seemed to preclude any return of the people, as though a passage would be opened for the captives but the Lord would find a road through regions where there was no road; the visible desert in which the Baptist preached was an image of that same hopelessness, so that in applying the prophecy to himself he does the prophet’s words no violence. Wesley sharpens the figure into a sound which dies into air once it has expressed the thought it signified, and is known no more. Robertson adds that the earliest writers marked the difference between Word for the Messiah and Voice for his herald. Gill records that Jewish commentators referred the crying variously to the Holy Ghost and to the archangel at the resurrection, one of them conceding that the comfort promised in the preceding verses belongs to the days of the King Messiah.
24:
Who the second deputation were, and why they are named, is the whole question. Gill describes the Pharisees as the strictest sect among the Jews, zealous for the traditions of the elders, professing to expect the Messiah, and famous in the nation for knowledge and learning. Wesley adds the temper that made them awkward questioners, peculiarly tenacious of old customs and jealous of any innovation unless the innovator could show unquestionable proof of divine authority — excepting, he notes drily, innovations brought in by their own scribes. Calvin states what the naming establishes: these were men who then held the highest rank in the Church, so that the evangelist is telling us the inquiry came not from contemptible persons of the Levitical order but from men clothed with authority. Barnes admits the reason for the mention is not certainly known, and observes that although many Sadducees had come to the baptism they do not seem to have joined in sending this delegation.

The grammar and the text are both pressed. Ellicott reports that the best manuscripts omit the relative, so that the verse becomes a statement that they had been sent from the Pharisees, and notes that the sentence stands where it does in order to explain the question which follows. Robertson parses the verb as a periphrastic past perfect passive and treats the phrase as giving the source of the committee. Origen reads the passage as a fresh mission rather than a continuation: the questions of the priests and Levites having been answered, another embassy comes, and so far as a conjecture may be formed from the discourse itself he takes this for the third occasion of questioning.

Origen then contrasts the two deputations by their manners. The earlier question, who are you, he calls mild and befitting the priestly and levitical character, with nothing arrogant or disrespectful in it, such as becomes true ministers of God; where the Pharisees, being a sectarian body as their very name implies, address the man importunately and contumeliously, asking why he baptizes at all — not caring for information but wishing to stop him. Origen notes the inconsistency that followed, since the very next thing they did was come to his baptism, and resolves it by their motive: they came not in faith but hypocritically, because they feared the people. Chrysostom offers a different account of the same party, that these were the same priests and Levites, being themselves Pharisees, who turned to accusation once blandishments had failed and they had forced him to say what he was not. Gregory adds the moral in a line, that a saint, even when perversely questioned, is never diverted from the pursuit of goodness.
25:
Why the baptism should be the sticking point is explained from Jewish practice, and the explanations differ in one detail. Barnes says baptism on receiving a proselyte from heathenism was common before this man’s time, but it was not customary to baptize a Jew, and he had changed the custom by baptizing all — which is what they wanted authority for. Clarke gives the same background and adds the procedural objection, that no proselyte entered the full privileges of a Jew until he was both baptized and circumcised, and that such baptisms were never performed except by an ordinance of the Sanhedrin. Wesley puts the double complaint plainly: without any commission from the council, and not only heathens but Jews also. Ellicott agrees the rite itself was probably already in use for proselytes and locates the strangeness elsewhere, that it is not baptism which puzzles the questioners but the footing on which he places it. Lightfoot supplies a further expectation, that the Jews looked for the world to be renewed at the Messiah’s coming, and quotes the lexicographers and the Gloss for the phrase about those years in which God will renew his world.

The form of their argument is examined by two. Calvin says that by laying down three degrees they appear to frame a conclusive case, since it does not belong to every man to institute such a practice, and the one who might do so would have to possess full authority. Robertson states the condition as a plain one and notes what it reveals of their estimate: they did not reckon his claim to be a voice important enough to justify the innovation. Origen asks a question of structure instead, whether the second testimony ends here and a third begins, addressed to those sent from the Pharisees, since what they wished to know was why he baptized at all if he was neither the Christ nor Elijah nor the prophet. He settles the matter by ranking the three testimonies according to what each asserts: the first declares the Saviour’s divinity, the second disposes of the suspicion of those who wondered whether the Baptist might himself be the Christ, and this third declares one already present among men though unseen by them, whose coming was no longer future.

Lightfoot assembles the expectations the question grew out of. The Jews looked for the purifying of the unclean, and he cites a rabbi on the promise to remove uncleanness by the sprinkling of the water of purification, and another for the tradition that Elijah would purify and restore the outcast, with a parallel saying that Elijah comes to distinguish the unclean and cleanse them. Seeing a man introduce so unusual a rite, by which Israelites themselves were admitted into a new rule of religion, they naturally asked by what authority he did it if he were neither the Messiah nor Elijah nor one of the prophets raised from the dead; and Lightfoot adds that their expectation of Elijah rested on a prophecy of Malachi not rightly understood.
26:
What the answer concedes and what it withholds is the point. Barnes notes that he did not deny the baptizing, nor condescend to state his authority for it: he admitted introducing an important change in the rites of religion, and went on to tell them this was not all, since greater things were coming. Gill takes the sense of the reply to be that he baptized in water, which was all he did or pretended to do. Clarke puts the distinction between form and end, that he used the common form while directing those he baptized to a different purpose, namely that they should repent of their sins and believe in the Messiah.

The clause about one standing among them is read for its force. Clarke identifies the person meant without hesitation. The weight of it, on every reading, falls on the contrast the verse sets up: a rite in water performed by a man who disclaims every title, set against a presence already in the crowd and unrecognised by the very people demanding his credentials — which turns their question back on them, since the authority they are looking for is standing where they are.

Origen reports a dissenting account of the sequence. Heracleon held a particular view of how these answers to the Pharisees’ messengers stand to what has gone before; and Origen, who has already disputed that writer’s attribution of an earlier verse, records and rejects his objection here. Heracleon held that the answers to the Pharisees’ messengers reply not to what was asked but to what the Baptist wished to say; Origen answers that this charges the prophet with a want of manners, making him answer about one thing when asked about another, and maintains instead that the reply takes the question up accurately. Asked why he baptizes if he is not the Christ, what other answer could be given than to show that his baptism was in its nature a bodily thing? The words about water meet the first half of the question, and the words about the one standing among them meet the second.

Calvin reads the reply as sufficient correction for anyone not deaf to it, since in sending them to Christ and declaring him present the Baptist proves not only that he was divinely appointed as Christ’s minister but that he is the true herald sent to testify that the time of the Church’s renewal had come. He notes that the contrast is left incomplete, the spiritual baptism of Christ not being expressly set against the external baptism here, though the missing clause is supplied shortly after. Robertson marks the tragedy in the words about their ignorance, and observes that so startling a declaration apparently excited no further inquiry from the committee. Ellicott thinks a passage of Ezekiel lies behind the phrase, with its contrast between water and spirit, and Wesley states the purpose of the rite, to prepare for the Messiah and to show that Jews as well as Gentiles must be washed from their sins.
27:
The two relations between the men are kept carefully apart. Calvin states both: Christ was behind him in the order of time, and far before him in rank and dignity, and a third statement about preference is soon added. Robertson makes the same distinction more briefly, that the forerunner has preceded the Messiah in time but not in rank, as he instantly goes on to say. Gill reads the coming after as true in two ways, both into the world and into the ministry of the word, John being earlier in each and greatly behind in everything else.

The clause about preference is a textual problem, and three of them say so. Clarke reports that it is wanting in a list of manuscripts and in the Coptic, Ethiopic, Slavonic and two copies of the Itala, and in some of the primitive fathers, and notes that Griesbach has left it out of his text. Ellicott goes further and treats the words as insertions made to harmonise this verse with the two places where the same thought occurs properly; omitting them, he says, leaves the one who comes after as the subject of the verb about standing, and the sentence reads continuously. Robertson notes that the article is absent in the chief manuscripts.

The image of the sandal is explained by its social weight. Barnes describes the latchet as the thong by which the sandal was fastened to the foot, and observes that to unloose it was a servant’s office, so that the Baptist means he is unworthy to perform the lowest service for the one coming. That reading makes the sentence a measure of distance rather than a compliment: the man who had just refused every title the deputation offered him now refuses even the standing of a slave in that presence, which is the strongest form the chapter has yet given to the difference between a voice and the one it announces.

Two further observations fix the measure. Barnes points out how unequal the comparison was at the time it was made: the Baptist was well known and highly honoured, thousands came out to hear him, and Jesus was as yet unknown, and it is this honoured man who declares himself unfit for the lowest service. Ellicott draws the practical conclusion for the deputation’s question, that the sentence is the warrant for the baptizing they had come to challenge, since the coming One is already standing in their midst and the herald’s own work is simply ministerial. Clarke adds that a group of manuscripts appends the promise of a baptism with the Holy Ghost and with fire at the end of the verse.
28:
The place-name is the chief question, and the answer is nearly unanimous against the received reading. Barnes reports that almost all the ancient manuscripts and versions have Bethany here rather than Bethabara, and calls that doubtless the true reading, noting that besides the Bethany two miles east of Jerusalem another is said to have lain in the tribe of Reuben. Clarke thinks it very probable that Bethany should be inserted, calls it in the judgment of the best critics the genuine reading, and sets out the authorities supporting it. Robertson calls Bethany beyond Jordan undoubtedly the correct text and explains the error, that Origen suggested the other name under the mistaken notion that the only Bethany was the one near Jerusalem. Ellicott tells the same story with the reason Origen gave: he found Bethany in almost all the copies but, unable to locate the place, concluded it must be the Bethabara he had heard of, where a local tradition held that the baptizing had been done. Origen himself records the state of the evidence, that he is aware of the reading found in almost all the copies and that it appears to have stood there earlier still.

Why the place is named at all is explained by two. Gill says simply that the testimony was borne and the discourse with the Pharisees held at a passage over Jordan where many people walked to go to the other side. Calvin reads the mention as doing two things: authenticating the narrative, and informing us that the answer was given before a numerous assembly, since many flocked to that baptism and this was the ordinary place for it. Chrysostom draws the moral from the circumstance, that boldness and freedom of speech are a great virtue, and the making of everything else secondary to the confessing of Christ so admirable a thing that the Only-begotten proclaims such a man in the Father’s presence.

Origen’s reasons are worth having in his own terms, since the whole later confusion rests on them. He had visited the places to enquire after the footsteps of Jesus and his disciples and the prophets; he found that the Bethany of Lazarus and his sisters lay fifteen stadia from Jerusalem and about a hundred and eighty from the Jordan, knew no other place of that name near the river, and was told that Bethabara was pointed out on its banks as the site of the baptizing. He then pressed the etymologies, house of preparation against house of obedience, the first suiting one who made ready a prepared people. Ellicott answers each limb: the argument from etymology is at best precarious, ignorance of a site after three hundred years of war and unsettlement is not unnatural, and a tradition favouring a place then popular for baptism is just what one would expect to grow, so that the critical judgment of one man cannot be preferred to the nearly unanimous copies.
29:
What the title claims, and how far the taking away reaches, is the matter of the verse. Gregory enters a limit at once: sin will be entirely taken from the human race only when our corruption has been turned to a glorious incorruption, since we cannot be free from it while we are held in the death of the body. Theophylact raises the grammatical question beside him, why the singular is used of the world’s sin. Augustine answers the harder form of the question, how a man can take away another’s sin at all: some say they do it because they are holy, and ask how a baptizer who is not holy could take away sin — and Augustine replies by locating the power elsewhere, in the one who did not take sin from our nature and therefore can take our sin away.

Origen reads the verse as marking a stage in the witness. After the preceding testimony Jesus is seen coming to the Baptist, who is not only persevering in his confession but advanced in goodness, which Origen takes to be intimated by the mention of a second day. The sequence matters to him because the testimonies have been graded through the chapter, and this one differs from those before it in having its object present and pointed out rather than described or denied.

Lightfoot grounds the title in the ritual. The law commanded the offerer to lay his hand on the head of the sacrifice, so transferring his guilt onto the victim, as is plainest in the scapegoat; and the same rite was used with the lamb of the daily sacrifice offered for all Israel, the substitutes of the people laying their hands upon its head. Barnes and Clarke gather the several lambs the phrase could evoke — the passover lamb eaten in remembrance of the deliverance from Egypt, the lamb of the morning and evening offering, the one led to the slaughter in Isaiah, and the lamb as an emblem of meekness — and Barnes insists the name rests on all of these together rather than on any one of them alone. Clarke sets out three respects in which this lamb differs from its types: it is God’s own provision and not man’s, it carries sin away in reality where the others did so representatively, and it carries away the sin of the world where they were offered for one people only. Calvin accounts for the figure, that John had to do with Jews accustomed to sacrifices who could be taught about atonement in no other way, and so lets one kind stand for the whole.

On the verb itself the readings converge. Ellicott notes that the margin’s beareth and the text’s taketh away together express the force of the original: he is ever taking sin away, and does it by bearing the burden himself. Robertson marks the singular rather than the plural, and a work still future described in the present tense, adding that he is the Lamb of God for the world and not for Jews only. Wesley compresses the clause into a sentence, that sin and the world are of equal extent. Chrysostom supplies the occasion for the words being spoken at all: having been baptized among the multitude, the Lord came again the next day so that none should suppose he had come as the others did, to confess sins and be washed to repentance, and the herald’s announcement corrected precisely that mistake.
30:
Ellicott counts the occurrences: these words meet us here for the third time, in full at verse fifteen and in part at verse twenty-seven, and each time as a quotation of an earlier and unrecorded saying of the Baptist, uttered in proverbial form and to be understood in its fulfilment. Robertson fixes the preposition — on behalf of whom, not merely concerning whom — and reads the sentence as spoken while the speaker points: this is he, there he is. Gill refers the earlier saying either to the previous day or to a time further back still, when the baptizing first began, before the Lord came to be baptized and before the two had met.

Calvin finds three assertions compressed into the sentence. The first, that a man comes after him, acknowledges his own priority in date: he went ahead to prepare the road, as Malachi had promised a messenger despatched in advance of the Lord’s face. The second, that this same man is made his superior, points to the glory with which God adorned his Son on entering the world to discharge a Redeemer’s office. The third supplies the ground of both, an eternal majesty, so that what the Father conferred was owed rather than accidental. Two conclusions follow: the speaker amounts to no more than a herald commissioned on another’s behalf, and the figure he announces is unmistakably the promised Christ.

Augustine compresses the same distinction into a line: he comes after me because he was born after me, he is made before me because he is preferred to me. Gregory supplies the ground of the preference, that he is not circumscribed by the time of his nativity, having been born of his mother in time and begotten of his Father out of time. Theophylact turns both to controversy. Against Arius he observes that the text does not say he was created before me but that he was before me; against the followers of Paul of Samosata, that one who derived the beginning of his being from the Virgin could not have been before a precursor who preceded him by six months in the order of human birth. The same commentator accounts for the word man as marking the mature age of thirty at the baptism, or in a spiritual sense the Spouse of the Church, in which sense Paul speaks of espousing a chaste virgin to Christ.
31:
The disclaimer is taken literally by most of them and explained from the two men’s circumstances. Gill glosses it by sight, as Nonnus paraphrases, and explains that though the two were related they lived at such a distance as to have no correspondence. The one was in the deserts until the day of his showing unto Israel, the other dwelt with his parents at Nazareth in a mean and obscure way, and the coming to Jordan for baptism was their first interview. Barnes puts the separation geographically, the hill country of Judea against the carpenter’s work at Nazareth; Clarke counts thirty years spent in the hill country of Hebron and places Nazareth on the extreme borders of Galilee; Wesley measures the distance at ninety miles or more and calls the whole arrangement a peculiar providence, surprising in view of how nearly the two were related and how remarkable the conception and birth of both had been.

What the separation was for is the point each of them presses. Gill says it was so ordered lest the high commendation should be thought to arise from the relationship, or from a confederacy and compact entered into between them. Barnes draws the same conclusion as proof that there could have been no collusion or agreement to impose upon the people. Wesley says plainly that acquaintance was prevented which might have made the testimony suspected. Calvin takes it further into the doctrine of ministry: the doubt is anticipated by affirming that the speaker had no knowledge of Christ except what he obtained by revelation, so that he speaks neither at his own suggestion nor for the favour of man; and since the parallel clause says he was sent, Calvin adds that only the calling of God makes lawful ministers, for whoever thrusts himself forward, whatever learning or eloquence he possesses, is entitled to no authority.

Ellicott dissents about how absolute the ignorance was. He renders it and I also knew him not, referring the words back to whom ye know not in verse twenty-six, and denies any inconsistency with the recognition at the approach to baptism: in the sense that the crowd did not know him standing among them, the Baptist did not know him either, though he must have been familiar with the incidents of the birth and earlier years and even with the features of the man. It cannot be, he says, that the Son of Mary was unknown to the son of Elizabeth; there must have been many wondering thoughts about that life, and the question whether it could be the life all looked for, answered each time by the little the Jewish idea of the Messiah found in the carpenter of a country village. Robertson leaves the personal question open and fixes instead on the purpose clause, that the whole ministry existed to manifest the Messiah’s presence to Israel, which is why the baptizing in water of those who confessed their sins stands in the same sentence.
32:
Chrysostom reads the verse as a proof offered under challenge. The declaration just made was astonishing to all who heard it, that the man pointed out did of himself take away the sin of the world, and the speaker might fairly be asked how he came to know it; so he answers beforehand by appeal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, naming the descent he had seen and the abiding that followed it.

Augustine blocks the inference that the descent was the beginning of anything. This was not the first occasion of the Lord’s receiving the unction of the Spirit; in it he condescended to prefigure his body the Church, in which those who are baptized pre-eminently receive the Spirit. To suppose otherwise is absurd, for it would mean that at thirty years of age he received the Spirit for the first time, and that he came to that baptism as destitute of the Spirit as he was of sin — when even of his servant and forerunner it is written that he should be filled. Elsewhere the same preacher sets himself to explain why God was pleased to manifest the Spirit in the form of a dove, and treats the question as owed to his hearers rather than as settled by the text.

Calvin handles the seeing.
