The expression is not literal but figurative, since with what eyes could the Spirit be seen; the visible sign being a certain and infallible mark of his presence, the name of the thing is transferred to the sign, exactly as Christ calls the bread his body. Such speech is frequent in the sacraments, and most defensible where the sign is at the same time a true and efficacious pledge by which we are made certain that the thing signified is bestowed. He then guards the figure from the opposite error: the dove did not contain him who fills heaven and earth, but he was present by his power, so that the exhibition was not presented to those eyes in vain.

Ellicott and Robertson both settle on the tense. Better, Ellicott says, I have seen or beheld: the vision is ever present in its result and is all-conclusive evidence. Robertson names the perfect middle and explains its force, that this sight of the Spirit descending became permanent proof to the man who saw it, even though the recognition of Jesus as Messiah had come earlier, when he came for baptism; he adds that the Semites regarded the dove as a symbol of the Spirit. Gill dates the record to the same day and the same discourse as what precedes, and Barnes and Clarke both pass the clause on to their notes at the parallel in Matthew rather than expound it twice.
33:
Barnes states exactly what the sign was for. The descending and abiding Spirit was the mark by which the Messiah was to be known, and it does not follow that there had been no earlier intimation: from the exchange at the baptism in Matthew it appears that the Baptist already supposed Jesus claimed to be the Christ and believed the claim, but the infallible and certain evidence was the descent itself, and the voice from heaven which declared the Son of God was something he heard and afterwards testified that he had heard. Gill makes the same distinction in his own way, placing the secret intimation and the promised signal before the coming to baptism, the one given to confirm the other.

Calvin raises the difficulty this creates and refuses the easy answer. If the man knew Christ, why did he decline to admit him to baptism, since to a stranger he would never have said that he himself had need to be baptized by him? Some reply that he knew him only so far as to revere him as a distinguished Prophet. Calvin calls that a poor solution, for every man owes obedience to the calling of God without respect of persons, and no rank or excellence in a human being should hinder anyone from doing his duty; had he spoken in that manner to any other person than the Son of God, he would have shown contempt for God and for the baptism entrusted to him. The ignorance the verse confesses must therefore be the kind that comes of personal and long acquaintance, not the absence of all recognition.

The commission behind the sign is where the rest settle. Clarke infers an intimate acquaintance with the Divine Being, the call and mission given at first and every subsequent direction given by immediate and unequivocal inspiration, and asks who is fit to proclaim Jesus but one who has continual intercourse with God and at all times abases himself that Jesus alone may be magnified. Robertson marks the emphatic pronoun that points back to God as the sender, and notes that the contrast between baptizing in water and baptizing in the Holy Spirit has to be filled in from the Synoptics. Cyril of Jerusalem explains the descent by the dignity of the one baptized, which was not to stay hidden: the heavens opened because of the dignity of him who came down, and the first-fruits of the Spirit promised to the baptized were fittingly conferred upon the manhood of the Saviour, who is himself the giver of that grace. Augustine, preaching on the same testimony, sets its authority on a different footing again — John is true, Christ is the Truth, and every true man is true only from the Truth.
34:
The tenses carry the argument, and Ellicott and Robertson both say so. Better, Ellicott renders, I have seen and have borne witness: the result of personal conviction was that the man testified at once and had not stopped doing so. One of the sayings he had taught his scholars was that this other existed before him, and the revelation at the baptism with the voice heard from heaven has now given that saying its true meaning, so that the teacher has himself learnt and the learner is now taught that Jesus is the pre-existent One. Robertson names the two perfects and takes the sight of the Spirit together with the Father’s voice hailing the Beloved Son as what stands behind the declaration.

Robertson then traces the title through the rest of the record. Nathanael uses it a few verses later as a Messianic title, and so does Martha; the Synoptic writers apply it to Christ; Caiaphas puts it to him under oath as a Messianic title and receives his confession, and he applies the term to himself repeatedly in this Gospel and by implication in the saying about the Father and the Son which the Synoptics also preserve. On that showing the Baptist’s words are not an isolated flight but the first use of a description the Lord accepted for himself.

Calvin draws out what the sign licensed the man to say. What he declares is not doubtful, because God was pleased to make him fully and thoroughly acquainted with the matters of which he was to be witness to the world; and the inference deserves notice, that whoever gives the Holy Spirit must be the Christ, since the honour and office of reconciling men to God belong to no other. Gill keeps to the bare fact, that he saw with his bodily eyes the Spirit descend from heaven as a dove, light upon Jesus and remain some time upon him. Wesley dates the testifying from that moment and no earlier. Augustine, preaching on this declaration, carries it straight into the congregation listening to him: the psalm’s cry of the needy and poor man is the voice not of one man and yet of one man — not of one, because the faithful are many grains groaning amid the chaff diffused throughout the whole world, and yet of one, because all are members of Christ and so a single body, whose grief and whose joy are alike within, where none sees but he who listens to the groaning and crowns the hoping.
35:
Gill makes it the third day from the visit of the priests and Levites, and observes that the Syriac, Arabic and Persic versions leave out the word again. Robertson counts the same third day from verse nineteen and parses the past perfect that does duty as an imperfect; Ellicott prefers was standing and reads the description as a scene present to the mind of one of the two disciples who was there. Barnes supposes the standing was apart from the multitude, and Clarke agrees with him in identifying Andrew as one of the pair and the writer of the Gospel as the other, adding that wherever he might have received honour he studiously conceals his own name.

Chrysostom asks why the herald waited by the river at all, instead of going about to preach in every part of Judea. The answer he gives is that the work was to be done by the works of Christ himself, and that the smaller method had the greater effect: a small spark was struck and suddenly rose into a flame. Had the man travelled and preached, it would have looked like human partiality and great suspicion would have been excited. Prophets and Apostles alike preached Christ absent, the one company before his appearance in the flesh and the other after his assumption; this man alone had to point him out by the eye and not by the voice only, which is why he is found standing where he could be seen pointing. Bede takes the standing itself for a figure, since the man had ascended that citadel of all excellences from which no temptation could cast him down, and his disciples stood with him as stout-hearted followers of their master.

Ellicott accounts for the two hearers without making them latecomers. There is no reason to think they had been absent the day before, with the testimony repeated specially for their benefit; rather, within that band there was an inner circle taught more because they could receive more. They had heard the words already, perhaps talked them over together, at least tried in private thought to follow them, and now they have come back to their teacher; and their teacher has himself passed through their struggle out of darkness into light, so that there is a Presence with them which he now knows and before which his own office must cease — the passing voice being no longer needed once the abiding Word has come. Chrysostom’s homily on the same scene presses the need for the repetition from the other side: human nature is slothful, not by its constitution but by deliberate choice, so that it needs much reminding, and what is said settles in the mind with difficulty, the ground being hard and entangled with innumerable thorns.
36:
Clarke takes the participle apart — from the preposition and the verb for looking, to view with steadfastness and attention — and makes the manner of looking the condition of seeing anything. At first sight the one pointed out appears only as a man among men, dying in testimony to the truth as many others have died; on more attentive consideration he appears no less than God manifest in the flesh, making by that death an atonement for the sin of the world. Ellicott says the word expresses a fixed, earnest gaze, and that at this look all the old thoughts come crowding back in their fulness. Robertson parses the aorist participle as antecedent to the saying, and finds in the present participle of walking a vivid picture of the speaker’s rapture, this being so far as we know the third and last glimpse he had of Jesus.

Gill supplies the hour and the gesture: it was towards the close of the day, the work was finished and the people departing home, and the eyes were fixed intently and with delight while the hand pointed. Barnes reads the look as a singling out, a regarding with special attention, a contemplating of the long-expected Deliverer of the world, and turns it into a rule for every minister to fix the eye on the Son of God and direct all others to him. Clarke adds what the pointing was for: to turn his own disciples to Jesus not only as the great sacrifice for the sin of the world but as the complete teacher of heavenly truth.

Calvin reads the repetition as a resignation of office. Perceiving that he was approaching the end of his course, the man laboured incessantly to hand his work over to Christ, and his firmness in doing so lends greater credit to what he says; by insisting so earnestly, through several successive days, on the same commendation, he shows that his own course was nearly finished. The same passage makes Calvin notice how small and low the beginning of the Church was. Disciples had been prepared, but only now does Christ begin to collect a Church, and he has no more than two men, mean and unknown — which serves to illustrate his glory, that within a short period, without human aid and without a strong hand, he spread his kingdom in so incredible a manner. And the chief object to which attention is directed in all this, Calvin observes, is the forgiveness of sins to be found in Christ.
37:
Chrysostom notices which words did the work. When the herald said that one coming after him was made before him, and that he was not worthy to unloose the latchet of his sandal, he gained over nobody; when he mentioned the economy and gave his discourse a humbler turn, announcing the Lamb of God, his disciples followed Christ. Many persons, Chrysostom explains, are less influenced by the thought of God’s greatness and majesty than by hearing of him as man’s Helper and Friend, or of anything pertaining to the salvation of men.

The same preacher turns the transfer into a bridal figure, and makes the silence part of it. While the announcement is made, Christ says nothing: the Bridegroom stands by without speaking, others introduce him and deliver the Bride into his hands, and he so treats her that she no longer remembers those who gave her in marriage. The friend of the Bridegroom came forth and put the Bride’s right hand in his, delivering men’s souls over by his preaching, and receiving them he so disposed of them that they returned no more. Alcuin states the sequence without the figure, that the disciples hitherto with the Baptist followed Jesus in obedience to their master’s word. Ellicott notices what is absent from the scene: no word severing the link between teacher and disciples, which would have been hard to speak and hard to hear, and no word bidding them follow, which cannot be needed.

Barnes finds the episode a proof of sincerity. The man was not desirous of forming a party or of building up a sect, and was willing that all whom his ministry had attracted to himself should become followers of Christ; from which Barnes argues that no minister should aim at his own interest or fame, but should be content that his disciples look to Christ rather than to him, and even forget him. Clarke presses the promptness instead: they perfectly understood their master’s meaning, and happy are those who on hearing of the salvation of Christ immediately attach themselves to its author, since delays are always dangerous and here often fatal. Henry adds the pedagogical point, that they had probably heard the same words the day before without effect, so that the benefit of repetition and of private personal converse appears in the difference. Wesley records how far their courage went — they walked after him, but did not venture to speak to him — and Robertson sums up the office now discharged, the Messiah predicted, portrayed, baptized, interpreted, and for a second time identified.
38:
Robertson pictures the moment from the grammar: the passive participle of turning renders the sudden act on hearing steps behind, and the question is not who but what purpose have you, these being the first words of Jesus preserved in this Gospel. Gill thinks the turning deliberate — he saw by their walk and their countenances that they were following, and knew it before he turned — done so that they might have an opportunity of speaking, or rather so that he might speak first. Ellicott describes the hesitation it relieved: they follow wishing and yet not daring to question him, and he draws them out by asking the first question himself, which they are unprepared for, since what they want is more than a passing interview.

Barnes insists the question was not asked for information, nor as a harsh reproof forbidding them to come, but as a kind inquiry after their desires and an invitation to lay open their minds; and he reads from it that the first inclinations of a soul towards Christ are regarded, and that ministers and other Christians ought to be accessible and tender towards all who are inquiring the way to life. Clarke supposes they felt some embarrassment after hearing the character their master had given, and that they were graciously accosted to prevent it; he then turns the question on his reader — what seek ye, in this place, in the company you frequent, in the conversation you engage in, in the works you perform — and reckons that such questions put home in the fear of God would alter much that is done and left undone.

The title they chose is treated as a datable word. Ellicott notes that in calling him Rabbi they placed themselves in the position of his scholars, though they had not yet learnt all they had been taught of his office; the word was the current title of a revered teacher, and the Baptist’s own disciples used it of him, but the writer remembers it as a modern term, known to Jews only since the days of Hillel and unlikely to be known to Greeks at all, and therefore translates it as he translates Messias and Cephas in the same section. Calvin adds that the name was commonly given to men of rank, and that the Evangelist points rather to the use of his own age for teachers and expounders of the word: the two do not yet own Christ as the only Teacher of the Church, but hold him for a Prophet and teacher, which is the first step towards being taught. Lightfoot presses the other half of their reply, whether asking where he lodged does not mean where he kept the sabbath, and reasons from the tenth hour that the little left of the day stood at about sunset and the entrance of a new one, so that abiding with him that night would have been the more natural way to put it.
39:
Barnes reads the reply as a refusal to postpone: he did not put them off to some future period, but was willing that they should come at once and have the full opportunity they wanted. Gill fills in the welcome, an invitation to go along directly and see with their own eyes where he lodged, and to converse with him then and at any other time. Robertson notes that the correct text has a promise rather than a command, that the preposition means at his side, and that the accusative of time covers the whole of that day. Ellicott marks what the writer withholds: they had been thinking of a visit later, perhaps on the following day, and are told to come now — yet we are not told where, nor given a hint of a word spoken, because this was the sacred turning-point of the writer’s own life, its incidents fixed at a depth no human eye may penetrate.

On the hour they divide, and the division is about which city’s clock the writer kept. Ellicott and Calvin both make it four in the afternoon: Ellicott finds no sufficient reason for supposing the Babylonian reckoning, usual at Ephesus as at Jerusalem, abandoned in this Gospel, and Calvin says simply that the evening was approaching, not more than two hours remaining till sunset, the twelve hours of the day being longer in summer and shorter in winter. Robertson takes the other side, that a writer at Ephesus late in the century naturally used Roman time, which puts it at ten in the morning and agrees with the evening of that day later in the book; and he adds that to his latest day the man never forgot the hour when he first met Jesus. Barnes sets out both computations and declines to decide. Calvin draws a conclusion from his own reading, that men so eager to hear Christ gave themselves no concern about a night’s lodging, where we incessantly delay because following is not convenient.

Clarke takes the invitation as a question he can answer for his reader. Where Christ dwells is not in the tumult of worldly affairs, nor in profane assemblies, nor in worldly pleasures, nor where drunkards proclaim their shame, nor in carelessness and indolence; he is found in his temple, wherever two or three are gathered in his name, in secret prayer, in self-denial, in fasting, in self-examination, and in the humble and contrite spirit. Those who do not know the salvation of God, he adds, would discover at that command that with him is the fountain of life, and that in his light they should see light.
40:
Ellicott notices that the veil is drawn here too. One of the pair is named, and he is Andrew, marked out already by the brother everyone knew; the other is left unidentified by a writer who keeps himself out of his own book. The same note takes in the shape of the day: on this first day, as the earnest of the harvest to come, there are two pairs of brothers, the sons of Zebedee and the sons of Jonas, who are afterwards always the leaders of the apostolic band. Robertson adds that the formal call of these four comes much later, by the sea in the Synoptic accounts, and parses the phrase about hearing as the classical idiom for hearing from a person, used elsewhere in this Gospel. Gill specifies what had been heard — the things spoken concerning Jesus as the Lamb of God.

Calvin states the Evangelist’s design for the rest of the chapter, which is to show how gradually the disciples were brought to Christ: Peter here, Philip and Nathanael afterwards. The immediate fetching of a brother expresses for him the nature of faith, which does not conceal or quench the light but spreads it in every direction; Andrew has scarcely a spark, and by means of that spark he enlightens his brother. Woe to our indolence, Calvin adds, if after being fully enlightened we make no attempt to bring others into the same grace. He matches the action against the two things Isaiah requires of the children of God, that each take his neighbour by the hand, and that he say, Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and he will teach us: the hand is stretched out here with exactly that object, that the two may be fellow-disciples in one school. Robertson adds that the man so introduced is heard from again later in the book, at the feeding of the multitude and when the Greeks ask to see Jesus, so that the brother of Peter is not merely a name used once to get Peter into the narrative, and Ellicott sends the reader to the apostolic lists for the remaining names.
41:
Chrysostom watches the haste. The words heard were not kept to himself; he ran to his brother to report good tidings, and though the Evangelist does not say what Christ had said to those who followed him, it can be inferred from what the brother repeats. In few words he declares what he had learnt, discloses the power of the Master who had persuaded them, and betrays his own earlier longing, the cry that they have found being desire turned to exultation now that the coming is real. Bede makes the double movement the test of it: truly to find the Lord is to love him fervently and to care for a brother’s salvation.

The name is handled as a translation problem with a history. Augustine lines up the three forms — Messias in Hebrew, Christus in Greek, Unctus in Latin — and explains that chrism is unction, that this one had a special unction which extended from him to all Christians, as the Psalm says that God anointed him with the oil of gladness above his fellows. Calvin says the Greek word is substituted to publish to the whole world what had been known in secret among the Jews: anointing was the ordinary mark of kings, yet they knew one King would be anointed by God under whom eternal happiness might be hoped for, and learned it the more clearly once David’s earthly kingdom proved impermanent. Of all the predictions Calvin finds Daniel’s the most forcible on this particular name, because he does not ascribe it to kings as the earlier prophets do but appropriates it to the Redeemer alone. Ellicott observes that the Hebrew form itself occurs in the New Testament only here and in the conversation at the well, both of them vivid pictures of remembered events, and Wesley notes that the interpretation is supplied here as it was for the title Rabbi.

Two small words carry a disputed inference. Ellicott argues that the only explanation giving adequate force to first and to his own is that each of the two went after his own brother, that Andrew found Peter first, and that the writer implies without stating that he found James himself, since stating it would have broken his reserve; the cry also implies a previous seeking, and that Simon was near enough to have heard the Baptist. Robertson sets out the textual alternatives, an adverb meaning that Andrew sought his brother before doing anything else, against a nominative adjective meaning he was the first of the two to do so; some old Latin copies read early in the morning, which Bernard prefers for allowing more time. Origen raises a different discrepancy, between the Simon found by his brother and renamed and the Simon seen walking by the sea of Galilee and called with his brother to catch men, and finds a fitness in the writer who tells of the Word becoming flesh recording the first and not the second.

Gill, Barnes and Clarke all take the errand as a specimen of what grace does. Gill describes the man affected with the grace bestowed on him, his heart warm from the conversation and transported with joy at having found the Messiah, going in all haste after his relations and acquaintance, because grace is of its nature communicative. Barnes puts it as a negative: religion does not monopolize itself or hide under a bushel, and does not wait for men to come but goes after them. Clarke says these men, having tasted the good word of Christ, were unwilling to eat their bread alone, and that whoever is brought to an acquaintance with God should bring at least one other, beginning with his own household. Chrysostom grounds it in creation, that the first man was not suffered to remain alone because great advantage comes of dwelling together, and that the same advantage holds between brothers.
42:
Robertson treats the new name as pure prophecy. The gaze is described by the same verb used of the Baptist’s own look a few verses earlier; the aorist of bringing is effective, as though some resistance on Simon’s part had to be overcome; and the name is given apparently before the man had spoken a word, in a future passive which predicts rather than confers — a byname that will fit him some day, though not yet, when he makes the noble confession and is told that he is Peter. Calvin says the same thing of the method: Christ names him not as men commonly do, from some past event or from what is now visible in him, but because he meant to make him what the name says. The father is named for the same reason, not out of honour but because the family was obscure and of no estimation, so that the obscurity may be seen not to hinder the making of a man of unshaken courage.

On the word itself the expositors fill in what the verse translates. Barnes identifies Cephas as the Syriac for what the Greek word means, a stone, and reads the rock as a symbol of firmness and steadiness — a trait very remarkable in the man after the ascension, where before the death of Jesus he had been rash, headlong and variable, so that the foresight is itself a proof of omniscience. He adds that the father’s name signifies a dove, which may be the point of the exchange: a name emblematic of timidity and inconstancy given up for one denoting constancy. Robertson distinguishes the two Greek words, the massive ledge of rock from the detached fragment of it, and notes that the Aramaic form is applied to Simon only here in the Gospels and otherwise only by Paul. Ellicott would print Peter in the text, since the writer was translating for Greek and not for English readers, and sets the renaming beside the Old Testament changes of Abram, Sarai and Jacob: he is now Hearer, the son of Jehovah’s grace, and shall be called a Rock-man.

Lightfoot defends the father’s name against those who would read it as John. Luke’s genealogy sounds that other name three different ways in Greek and never in this form; Jonah was a name very commonly used among the Jews and appears frequently in the Talmudic authors; and this son of Jonah imitated the prophet of that name in two particulars, that both preached to Gentiles and both began their journey from Joppa. Gill reads the bringing as zeal and brotherly affection at once: he would not have his brother rest in the bare account given him, but have him go and be personally acquainted and instructed; and the readiness was on both sides, since Simon rose up at once and went, which shows how one person may be the means of bringing another.
43:
Chrysostom notices the order in which the first disciples were gathered. No one was called before some had joined of their own accord, and not without reason, since an invitation issued before anyone had come might have made them start back. Philip is then the exception that proves the rule: Andrew had been persuaded by what he heard from the Baptist and Peter by Andrew, but Philip learned nothing from any man, was told only to follow, and straightway obeyed without going back, becoming a preacher to others. The cry that they have found belongs always, Chrysostom says, to men who have been seeking, and it betrays a thoughtful mind assiduously meditating on the writings of Moses and expecting the Advent.

Alcuin reads the journey allegorically. Judea is left, where the baptizing was going on, out of respect to the Baptist, so as not to appear to lower his office while it lasted; and the going forth is into a place whose name he takes for transition or revelation, so that as the Lord himself increased in wisdom and stature and favour, suffered, rose, and entered his glory, he would teach his followers to go forth, increase in virtue, and pass through suffering into joy. Whoever imitates his humility and suffering in order to partake of his resurrection follows him in that sense. The town named in the next breath means house of hunters, which Alcuin takes as an allusion to the future office of these particular men, the catching and saving of souls.

The date and the apparent clash with Matthew are handled together. Ellicott makes it the fourth day from the inquiry of the Sanhedrin, the finding happening as the Lord set out from his lodging, and observes that Philip appears in the other Gospels only in the lists of the Twelve, every touch of his character being preserved here. Robertson counts the same fourth day, notes the dramatic present, and thinks the meeting not accidental but possibly owing to the efforts of Andrew and Peter. Barnes removes the difficulty directly: this is not the call to the apostolate, which took place at the Sea of Tiberias, but the moment of conviction that he was the Christ, so that Matthew records the time of the commission and this writer the time of first acquaintance, with no contradiction between them. Clarke gathers what tradition reported of the man — a native of Bethsaida, married with several daughters on Eusebius’s account, a preacher in the two Phrygias — and warns against confounding him with Philip the deacon.

Ellicott weighs the two words of the command. They are never used in the Gospels except as spoken by the Lord himself, and are addressed to only one man outside the apostolic circle, the rich young man whom Jesus loved; elsewhere in the New Testament they occur once, in the angel’s word to Peter in prison. They cannot therefore be reduced to an invitation to come along on that day’s walk, though that is included, since in the walk itself came the revelation which made the command binding for a whole life. Calvin infers from the effect of a single word how great the efficacy of God’s word is, and then enters the qualification: it does not work indiscriminately in all, for God addresses many without advantage, as though striking their ears with a sound that vanished into air, and external preaching is in itself unfruitful except that it wounds the reprobate mortally and leaves them inexcusable. Only where the secret grace of God quickens it are the senses so affected that a man is ready to go wherever he is called. Henry adds that God has various methods of bringing his chosen ones home and is tied to none of them, and that this one was called in a preventing way, found before he had made any enquiry at all.
44:
Ellicott counts the clause among the minute touches of local knowledge which give this Gospel the colour that only an eye-witness could impart, and makes it do two pieces of work. It explains the meeting, since Philip was going home and the town lay on the road the Lord would naturally take towards Cana; and it explains how he passed from Messianic hope to settled belief, for he was a fellow townsman of Andrew and Peter, men who had talked together of ancient prophecy and future expectation, and one of whom had announced the discovery in striking language — the very word Philip now uses to Nathanael. Robertson separates the two places of the name, the Julias in Iturea on the eastern side of the lake and the western one in Galilee, perhaps near Capernaum, and settles on the latter because a later chapter adds of Galilee; he also thinks the townsmen’s example inclined Philip to do as they had done. Gill describes the town itself, on the lake of Gennesaret, afterwards made a city by Philip the tetrarch and renamed for Caesar’s daughter, a fishing place named from that trade, whose disciples followed that business.

Calvin asks why the name is recorded at all, and answers that it displays the goodness of God to these three the more illustriously. Christ elsewhere threatens and curses that city severely, so that when God brought some into favour with himself out of a place so ungodly, we ought to regard it as if they had been fetched out of the lowest hell; and when, having drawn them from that gulf, he honours them so far as to make them Apostles, the favour is distinguished enough to be worth recording. Barnes is content to note that this was the town where Andrew and Peter also lived.

The two accounts do not quite agree about which town was which. Gill applies the refounding by the tetrarch and the name Julias to the very place the disciples came from, where Ellicott and Robertson keep that city on the eastern shore and in another province and reserve the western Bethsaida of Galilee for Philip and his townsmen. Ellicott cites Josephus for the eastern city and Robertson the feeding narrative that belongs to it, so that on their reading the fishing village and the tetrarch’s foundation are two places whose shared name has caused the trouble.
45:
Who the man was occupies most of them. Ellicott and Robertson agree that the name is the Hebrew of the Greek Theodorus, God’s gift, preserved in our Theodore and Dorothea, and that he came from Cana, the very town the Lord was making for, so that Philip probably travelled with him and found the man at or near home. Both also hold him to be Bartholomew under another name, Robertson because this name is absent from the Synoptics and that patronymic absent from this Gospel. Clarke sets out the reasons at length: the evangelists who name the one say nothing of the other and the reverse; no notice is taken anywhere of Bartholomew’s vocation; Bartholomew is not a proper name at all but means son of Ptolomy; and this writer ranks Nathanael with the apostles at the lakeside after the resurrection. Gill adds a Syriac dictionary that simply calls him Bartholomew, and the form Nathanael bar Tholmai; Wesley argues from the order of the lists, that Matthew joins Bartholomew to Philip while this Gospel puts Nathanael immediately after Thomas, exactly where Bartholomew stands in Acts.

What Philip actually said is weighed next. Robertson notes that he borrows the cry of the earlier finder, and so joins himself to the circle of believers, but describes rather than names, putting the man of whom Moses in the law and the prophets wrote in place of the title Messiah. Barnes and Clarke both supply the texts meant, the prophet like Moses in Deuteronomy, the sceptre not departing from Judah, the seed of the woman, and from the prophets the suffering servant and the seventy weeks. Barnes observes that the description followed common apprehension: they spoke of him as Joseph’s son because he was commonly supposed to be, and as belonging to Nazareth, though they may not have been ignorant of the birth at Bethlehem. Ellicott presses that nothing can be argued from the words about such ignorance, since they are Philip’s and not the writer’s, and a man a few hours in that company might well not yet have heard it. Wesley says bluntly that Philip thought so, not knowing of Bethlehem.

Calvin counts the errors and lets them stand. The measure of Philip’s faith appears in this, that he cannot say a few words about Christ without mingling two gross mistakes, the parentage and the native town, both of them false; and yet, because he sincerely desires to do his brother good and to make Christ known, God approves the diligence and even crowns it with success. Calvin adds that proud men may despise such feeble beginnings of the Church, though a brighter display of the divine glory is to be seen in them than if the kingdom had been splendid from the outset, since we know to how rich a harvest that small seed grew; and he marks the modesty of a man who wants nothing except to have others learn beside him from a Teacher common to all. Robertson’s aside runs the other way and is a reproach to his own age: here one wins one, and now it takes a hundred to win one.
46:
Ellicott insists on the exact form of the objection: it is not whether the Messiah can come out of Nazareth, but whether any good thing can. He hears it from a man of a neighbouring village looking on a familiar town with something of local jealousy, though the wording seems also to point at an ill repute attaching to its people; the place is unknown to earlier history and is not named even by Josephus, while what Mark and Luke report of it agrees with the speaker’s opinion. Robertson finds the same tinge of scorn in the town’s name standing first in the sentence, allows that rivalry between neighbouring villages may account for part of it, and concludes that the man had clearly never heard of Jesus; a saying had grown up that no prophet comes out of Galilee, untrue like many such sayings, and the best thing in the world came out of Nazareth without Philip pausing to argue the point.

Clarke canvasses three explanations of the phrase. Bishop Pearce would give the words a particular force from Jeremiah, where God promises to perform that good thing and explains it as causing the branch of righteousness to grow up to David, so that the question implies Bethlehem rather than Nazareth as the appointed birth-place, just as the chief priests and scribes afterwards determined. Failing that, Clarke supposes either that the town had become so abandoned that its wickedness had passed into a proverb, or that the question is merely illiberal and full of national prejudice. Gill takes the first line, that the mention of Nazareth at once stumbled a man who knew very well that Bethlehem was to be the place of the birth; Barnes takes the second, that the character of the town was proverbially bad and that to call a man a Galilean or a Nazarene was an expression of decided contempt.

Barnes then uses the question against a habit of mind: this was judging not by examining evidence but by prejudice, as men do who let their minds be filled against religion and pronounce without examination, when in truth it matters nothing where a teacher comes from provided he be authorized of God and qualified for his work. Wesley says how cautiously popular prejudices should be guarded against, since these had possessed so honest a heart as to make him suspect Jesus of imposture, and credits the man’s integrity with prevailing over the bias and laying him open to evidence. Calvin names two faults in one breath, that he rashly believed what Philip had put incorrectly, and that a preconceived opinion about the place held his mind, so that a holy man came near to shutting himself out from Christ altogether — which is how Satan works daily, spreading falsehoods to raise suspicion of the Gospel and, failing that, trying to make Christ himself look contemptible. Barnes calls the reply the best possible answer, since Philip neither reasoned nor speculated about the possibility but sent the man to examine for himself, and Robertson notes that in doing so he followed his Master’s own method of the day before, probably without knowing it. Ellicott hears in the two words the fulness of Philip’s own conviction, an interview having settled his mind and being likely to settle another’s, while Lightfoot observes that nothing is commoner in the Talmudic authors than the same phrase.
47:
Chrysostom reads the earlier objection as a credential. The difficulty about Nazareth showed how carefully the man had read the Scriptures, and his not rejecting the tidings when they were brought showed how strongly he desired the coming; he had supposed Philip mistaken about the place, not the person. So there was no fault to find with him though he had spoken like one who did not believe, since he was more deeply read in the Prophets than Philip was; and he is called guileless because he had said nothing either to gain favour or to gratify malice.

Augustine turns the word over and refuses the flattering sense. What does it mean that no guile was in him — had he no sin, was no physician necessary for him? Far from it, since no one was ever born of a temper that did not need the Physician. Guile is saying one thing and thinking another; and there was none here because this sinner confessed his sin, where a sinner who pretends otherwise is precisely the man with guile in him.

Robertson and Ellicott both hear the patriarch behind the sentence. Truly an Israelite, Robertson glosses, one living up to the covenant name, Israel at its best, without the guile Jacob once had and Isaac complained of, the very word standing in the Greek of that passage in Genesis, as it does of the servant who was to have no deceit in his mouth. Ellicott makes the link explicit — behold one true to the name of Israel, in whom there is nothing of the Jacob — and asks what gave the sentence that shape: whether under the shade of a tree, where Jews were accustomed to retire for meditation and prayer, the history of Jacob had been present to the man’s mind, whether he too was left alone, and whether he prevailed with God. Lightfoot presses the same retirement from the other side: he was certainly not sleeping or idling there, which would have deserved no such encomium, but had sequestered himself for prayer or reading so thoroughly out of sight that he must needs own Jesus as Messiah for that very reason, that one who could not have been seen by any mortal eye knew where he was; and the praise sets that privacy against the usual craft of men who prayed in the streets to be seen.

Barnes and Clarke keep the commendation modest, and Calvin generalises it. Barnes reads an Israelite not by birth only but one worthy of the name, with the spirit and integrity becoming a man who fears God and obeys his law, and insists the words do not say he was without sin but that he had no disguise and made no profession he did not live up to. Clarke, less charitable to the nation, calls deceitfulness its deeply marked characteristic, so that a man walking uprightly in the midst of so much corruption was a subject worthy the attention of God himself. Calvin says the praise is not bestowed for the man’s own sake but holds out a general doctrine under his person: since many who boast of believing are far from believers, some mark is needed by which the genuine may be told from the false. The nation gloried haughtily in Abraham and boasted of the holiness of its descent while scarcely one in a hundred was not degenerate; and so a short definition here tears the mask from hypocrites, and at the same time disarms beforehand the offence of seeing those who claimed to be children of Abraham turn into the deadliest enemies of the Gospel.
48:
Gill measures the surprise precisely. What startled the man was not being named, nor having his town told him, but hearing a stranger hit on his general character and describe the internal frame of his soul — a thing ordinarily learnt only from long and familiar acquaintance. The reply betrays no doubt about the description itself, which any good man is conscious of in his own case; only amazement at how it could be known. Barnes and Clarke both explain the question by his not yet being acquainted with the divinity of the speaker, whom he took for a stranger, and Clarke draws the double moral, that it is the comfort of the sincere and upright that God knows their hearts, and should be the terror of the deceitful that their false dealing never escapes the all-seeing eye. Robertson adds that he had overheard the tribute and longed to know its source.

The tree is where the expositors do their work. Barnes infers that the judgment of character rested on something which happened there, though what is not recorded, and supposes a habit of retiring to the shade of a particular tree, in a garden or a grove, for meditation and prayer, the Jews being much given to choosing such places and the Saviour himself worshipping in them. Clarke notices the article — not a fig tree but the fig tree, one distinguished from the rest — and reports many proofs that the rabbins chose the shade of trees, and that tree in particular, to sit and study under. Robertson observes that the tree was a familiar object in that country and probably in leaf at the season, that the case governed by the preposition may itself suggest withdrawal for prayer, and that what was seen was the worship and not merely the presence. Ellicott sets the scene at the man’s own house, under the fig tree of his own garden, where and not at the corners of the streets he was praying in the honesty of his heart, unseen as he supposed by any eye and seen by the one to whose coming every true Israelite looked.

Calvin explains why the answer answers. Christ did not mean to flatter him, but did mean to be heard, so as to draw out a further question whose reply would prove him the Son of God; and the question was reasonable enough, since a man free from all deceit is an uncommon thing to meet with, and to know such purity of heart belongs to God alone. Calvin grants that the reply looks beside the point, for it does not follow from seeing a man under a tree that one can penetrate the secrets of his heart, and then supplies the missing link: as it belongs to God to know men when they are not seen, so it belongs to him to see what is not visible to the eyes, and since this seeing had plainly not been after the manner of men but by a look truly divine, the hearer could conclude that the speaker was not speaking as a man. Ellicott reaches the same point from the other side, that on this reading the meeting was not the first, an actual Messianic presence having already been at work in the man’s inmost thought.
49:
Barnes and Clarke take the three titles one at a time. Rabbi is Master, or better Teacher, a word Clarke thinks should simply be translated. By Son of God, Barnes argues, the Messiah is meant: conscience had told the man that the description of him was true, and therefore that the speaker must know the heart and its desires, which no mere man could do. King of Israel was another of the titles under which the Messiah was expected, and the one afterwards affixed to the cross; Clarke glosses it as the real descendant of David, to sit on that spiritual throne of which David’s was the type. Wesley calls the whole a confession of the person and the office together, and reckons happy those who are swift to receive the truth and grace of God. Robertson refuses to tone the confession down: the man was a student of the Old Testament, as Philip’s way of approaching him implied, and was quick to put his reading together with Philip’s report and the supernatural knowledge just displayed; and though the second title may strike us as an anti-climax after the first, both stand together as Messianic in the second Psalm, and the same title greets him at the entry into Jerusalem.

Chrysostom raises a difficulty and says plainly that it is not a small one. The depth of the Scriptures is not to be discovered carelessly or in our sleep, but needs close search and earnest prayer; and here is a question requiring real zeal. Peter made this identical confession after many miracles and much high doctrine, and was called blessed as one who had received the revelation from the Father; this man says the very same thing before seeing a miracle or hearing a discourse, and no such word is spoken to him — he is asked instead whether a word about a fig tree is what made him believe, and told he shall see greater things than these.

Calvin asks why the kingship follows from the divine knowledge, since the two do not look necessarily connected. His answer is that the man takes a loftier view: he had already heard that this was the Messiah, and he adds to that report the confirmation just given him, holding besides the principle that such a one does not come without exercising a King’s office over the people of God. From this Calvin draws a rule about faith, that it ought not to be fixed on the essence of Christ alone but should attend to his power and office, since it profits little to know who Christ is without knowing what he means to be towards us and why the Father sent him; and he charges his opponents with keeping no more than a shadow of Christ because they examined his bare essence and let the office go. Ellicott describes the instant rather than reasoning about it, as recognition begetting recognition: the Presence the man had felt as a spiritual power, quickening hope and thought and making the prophets’ words living truths, goes through him again and is now standing in front of him.
50:
Gill and Calvin both deny that the words are a rebuke. Gill reads them as approval and surprise, not as a reproof of a man too credulous, who had given in to belief on single expressions; Calvin says the same and adds what the sentence does instead, promising to this man and to others that the faith will be confirmed by stronger arguments. Ellicott points out that the clause need not be read as a question at all, and that a fuller sense comes of taking it as a statement: on this evidence you believe, and the exercise of the faculty strengthens it. He compares the same word later in the book, in the saying to the disciples before the passion and in the word to Thomas, where a statement rather than a question is likewise the better reading.

Barnes says what the greater things are — fuller proof of the Messiahship, and particularly what the next verse promises. Clarke paraphrases the whole: since you have credited my divine mission on the simple proof that I saw you when and where no human eye placed where mine was could have seen you, your faith shall not rest on that alone, for you shall have more numerous and express proofs of my eternal power and Godhead. Robertson works on the wording, noting that the redundant pair of verbs occurs in the Synoptics and in the Greek of the Old Testament and belongs to the vernacular, so that it is no evidence of an Aramaic original as Burney had argued; he marks the causal conjunction at the head of the sentence and the comparative with its ablative, and leaves one small point open, that the second conjunction before the verb of seeing may be declarative or merely recitative, either making sense here; the man’s wonder, he remarks, no doubt grew as the speaking went on.

Calvin then notices the change of address, and makes it the point of the verse. Being seen while absent and at a distance was peculiar to one man; the proof now brought forward would be common to all, so that, as if breaking off from what he had begun, the speaker leaves off addressing an individual and turns to address everyone standing there.
51:
The doubled word is handled as a question of idiom and of authority. Ellicott notes that this is its first occurrence, that the reduplicated form appears nowhere in the New Testament outside this Gospel, that it is always spoken by the Lord and attached to some deeper truth, and that it answers to a Hebrew word twice doubled in the Old Testament; in the Apocalypse the same word serves as a proper name of the faithful and true witness. Robertson adds that the repetition belongs only to the words of Jesus and illustrates his authoritative manner, and that the plural pronoun here, after a singular one just before, shows others besides Nathanael addressed. Lightfoot asks why the doubling stands here and not in the other evangelists, and offers three answers: that the asseveration may not belong to the same matters or occasions; that a writer working for Hellenists may have set the word down both as Christ used it and as Greeks used it; and that where others put it at the end of a sentence, the Lord puts it only at the beginning, as being himself the Amen, so that his single Amen elsewhere already contained the doubling. Gill makes that last point his own, and Barnes defines the word from the verb to confirm, adding that the repetition expresses the speaker’s sense of the weight of what he says.

On the opened heaven the readings converge on Bethel. Barnes warns that the seeing may not be with the bodily eyes but a having of evidence that the thing is so, treats the opened heaven as a figure for the conferring of favours, as in the Psalm where its doors were opened and manna rained down, and finds an evident allusion to the ladder of the dream, while doubting that any literal opened sky is promised. Robertson parses the perfect participle as standing open, grants that the words recall the baptism, but makes the immediate reference the opened heaven as a symbol of free intercourse between God and man, afterwards illustrated in the death of Stephen; the quotation is from the vision at Bethel, which was a dream to Jacob, where Christ is himself the bond of fellowship between heaven and earth. Clarke offers two senses: that a clear and abundant revelation of God’s will is now to be made, the mysteries shut up from eternity concerning man’s salvation fully disclosed; and that the ascending and descending signifies a perpetual intercourse opened through the Mediator, a metaphor he takes from the despatching of couriers between a prince and his ambassador abroad.

When this is to be seen divides them. Calvin thinks those greatly mistaken who inquire anxiously after the place and the time, since what is pointed out is something perpetual, always to exist in the kingdom: he allows that the disciples saw what is not seen today, and that the glory manifested at the ascension differed from anything we now behold, but holds that what happened then is of perpetual duration, because the kingdom once closed against us stands actually open in Christ — as the instances given to Stephen, to the three on the mountain, and to the disciples at the ascension showed. Wesley takes the opposite line, that those who believe now in the state of humiliation shall hereafter see him come in his glory with all the angels, allowing that the words may instead refer to the ascension. Ellicott supplies the textual ground of the dispute: the word rendered hereafter is omitted by several ancient authorities, the Sinaitic and Vatican manuscripts among them, yet has early evidence for its insertion, and since dropping it removes a difficulty of interpretation the omission is probably to be traced to that convenience; retained, it is better rendered henceforth. He adds that the preceding words were spoken to one man where this promise is made to all present.
